scenarios.name: Setup: every seat starts at score 0 and puddings 0, hand 1, full 104-card deck
Deal with 4 players: 8 cards each leave the deck (72 left), one picked so 7 remain in hand (any cards)
Deal with 3 players: 9 cards each leave the deck (77 left), one picked so 8 remain in hand (any cards)
Deck is not reshuffled: after a full hand and the next deal, 104-32-32=40 cards remain
Every seat is asked to pick from its own hand only
A single card in hand is taken automatically with no question and the hand empties
A revealed pick leaves the hand and goes to the tableau
Tempura, Sashimi and Dumpling picks count toward their sets (2nd tempura 5, 3rd sashimi 10, 3rd dumpling 6)
Maki-3/1/1 add icons: totals 3,2,1,0 give 6 and 3
Pudding adds 1 and puddings survive the end of a hand
Wasabi picked earlier triples the next nigiri; passing decides who gets what
Nigiri without wasabi: Egg 1, Salmon 2, Squid 3
Nigiri on wasabi: Egg 3, Salmon 6, Squid 9
Remaining hand passes left: seat 1's leftover Pudding reaches seat 2
Tempura: 3 gives 5, 4 gives 10, 1 gives 0
Sashimi: 5 gives 10, 6 gives 20, 2 gives 0
Dumplings: 1,4,5,6 score 1,10,15,15
Nigiri points are scored; unused wasabi scores nothing
Three-way tie for most maki splits 6 as 2 each; no second place
Single maki leader gets 6; two tied seconds get floor(3/2)=1 each
Two tied for most maki get 3 each and the next player gets nothing
Players with 0 maki score no maki points even when only one other has maki
Hand counts reset after a hand (all-Wasabi second hand scores nothing) while puddings stay
End of game: sole pudding leader gets +6, two tied fewest get -3 each
End of game: two tied for most puddings get +3 each and share the win
End of game: 0 puddings counts as fewest; two seats at 0 get -3 each
End of game: equal puddings score nothing
Game ends after the last pick of hand 3 with 3 players (pick 27)
Game ends after the last pick of hand 3 with 4 players (pick 24)
Score tie broken by most puddings
Players tied on score and puddings share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer suggests 4, and hand sizes are defined only for 3 and 4. At 3, passing still creates drafting tension. Above 4 the rules give no hand size.
The source says there is no talk phase. Drafting is decided by reading the visible tableaus and passed hands.

A thoughtful player tracks what others are collecting and what will come back around, denies key cards to rivals, times wasabi before high nigiri, and weighs the pudding race against points in each hand.
There are at most 10 puddings, so puddings can never outweigh one point of score. Players still tied share the win, matching the source's draw.

spec_choices.what: Dumpling table written as m*(m+1)/2 with m = min(dumplings,5)
spec_choices.why: This gives exactly 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 and is pure arithmetic.

simplifications.what: The left neighbour is the next seat number, wrapping to seat 1
simplifications.why: The engine has no physical seating.

simplifications.what: Passing is done by rotating the hand lists between players in one update
simplifications.why: The engine moves cards only through list operations.

simplifications.what: The automatic last pick is done as an update instead of a question
simplifications.why: The rules take the single card without a choice.

variation.original_summary: Sushi Go is a 2-5 player card-drafting game over 3 hands. Each turn everyone secretly keeps one card from their hand and passes the rest to the left. Sets of sushi (tempura, sashimi, dumplings, maki, nigiri with wasabi, pudding) score by arithmetic, and the highest total after 3 hands wins.

review.evidence: Simple policies all lose to adaptive play. 'Always take the card worth the most points right now' ignores sets: half a tempura pair or one sashimi scores 0. 'Always chase sashimi' gives 0 when a neighbour takes the third copy. 'Always take dumplings' depends on how many others want them. 'Always grab maki' splits the 6 points when contested. 'Ignore pudding' risks -6. Seats are symmetric because every hand rotates past every player.

Drafting greatly reduces deal luck, since you see most hands in the round. Still, the shuffle decides which sets are available, and with 4-5 players a weaker player's choices change what the stronger player is passed, which adds noise. Chopsticks adds a swingy extra pick. Skill wins over a series but not every game.

A beginner who collects obvious sets still scores 20-30 points per hand. Strong play adds several layers: remembering hands already seen, predicting what the left neighbour will take, denying sets ('hate drafting'), timing wasabi, and judging the maki and pudding majorities across hands.

Hands are hidden, but you have seen earlier versions of the hands now held by others. You must infer what is still circulating, model which cards each neighbour needs from their face-up cards, and plan over the hand (will a third sashimi come back?) and over the game (pudding majority).
Every score comes from counts of cards: set sizes, majority comparisons and multipliers. No judgement is needed.

The game is turn-based, text-only and uses no board. However, chopsticks needs a second pick inside a turn and a card returned into a hand that is being passed, which is a conditional extra block of steps. The 2-player variant needs a special pudding rule. With 5 players there are many steps per player, and hand sizes change with player count.

problems: P1: Chopsticks needs a conditional second pick within a turn and returns the card into the hand being passed, which the flat step list cannot express cleanly. It also adds swingy extra picks.

P2: The 2-player game needs a special no-penalty pudding rule, and in 2 players the highest-total rule makes play pure hate-drafting. The 5-player game adds noise from passing chains and almost uses up the deck.

P3: The rules are vague in places: maki tie-breaking beyond the split, what happens when a wasabi never gets a nigiri, how ties for fewest pudding work, and how a final tie is resolved after the pudding tie-break.
P4: Pick order and hand-size bookkeeping vary with player count, which raises build complexity and the number of steps.
P5: Moderate luck from the shuffle and from passing chains weakens how reliably skill decides the winner.

changes.what: Remove chopsticks from the deck (104 cards remain, with the original proportions of everything else).
changes.why: Every turn becomes exactly one simultaneous pick, so no conditional block of steps is needed. A swingy luck source disappears.
changes.fixes: P1: Chopsticks needs a conditional second pick within a turn and returns the card into the hand being passed, which the flat step list cannot express cleanly. It also adds swingy extra picks.

changes.what: Restrict the game to 3 or 4 players (4 suggested): 9-card hands for 3 players and 8-card hands for 4.
changes.why: This avoids the special 2-player pudding rule and the degenerate head-to-head denial game. It keeps the deck sufficient and the number of rounds at 27 or fewer. With 4 players every hand passes each player twice, which rewards memory and inference.
changes.fixes: P2: The 2-player game needs a special no-penalty pudding rule, and in 2 players the highest-total rule makes play pure hate-drafting. The 5-player game adds noise from passing chains and almost uses up the deck.

changes.what: Spell out every scoring edge case: maki ties, unused wasabi, pudding ties including the case where all are tied, players with zero cards, and a final tie-break chain ending in a shared draw.
changes.why: The winner must follow by arithmetic with no interpretation left to a referee.
changes.fixes: P3: The rules are vague in places: maki tie-breaking beyond the split, what happens when a wasabi never gets a nigiri, how ties for fewest pudding work, and how a final tie is resolved after the pudding tie-break.

changes.what: Make each engine round one pick turn with a fixed sequence of steps. Hands are dealt only on the first pick of each hand (the single random draw that round). Set scoring happens only on the last pick of each hand, and pudding scoring only on the last pick of the game.
changes.why: This keeps the game to one choice, one random draw and about 17 steps per round, with conditions only on single steps.
changes.fixes: P4: Pick order and hand-size bookkeeping vary with player count, which raises build complexity and the number of steps.

changes.what: Each turn, publicly announce every player's face-up cards and the number of cards in each hand. Privately show each player their current hand.
changes.why: Players have everything needed to reason about neighbours' needs. Skill then shows in inference and denial rather than in tracking bookkeeping, which reduces noise from misreading the state.
changes.fixes: P5: Moderate luck from the shuffle and from passing chains weakens how reliably skill decides the winner.

keeps: Simultaneous secret pick from a hidden hand, then pass the rest to the left
Three hands with puddings carried across hands
All original sushi scoring: tempura pairs, sashimi triples, the dumpling ladder, maki majorities, nigiri values tripled by wasabi, and the pudding majority and minority
Highest total wins, with puddings as the tie-break

recommendation.reason: The core drafting loop is already a strong hidden-information, opponent-modelling game. It needs only the removal of chopsticks, fixed player counts and fully specified scoring to fit the engine.

variation.name: Sushi Draft
variation.summary: A 3-4 player Sushi Go without chopsticks. Over three hands, players secretly keep one card at a time from a hidden hand and pass the rest left, building scoring sets while reading and denying their neighbours.
variation.rules:
DECK (104 cards): 14 Tempura, 14 Sashimi, 14 Dumpling, 6 Maki-1 (1 maki icon), 12 Maki-2 (2 icons), 8 Maki-3 (3 icons), 10 Salmon Nigiri, 5 Squid Nigiri, 5 Egg Nigiri, 10 Pudding, 6 Wasabi.

SETUP: Shuffle the deck once at the start of the game. Every player starts with a score of 0 and 0 puddings. The game has 3 hands. Each hand has 9 picks with 3 players or 8 picks with 4 players, so the game lasts 27 or 24 rounds. One round is one pick.

EACH ROUND:
1. Deal (first pick of a hand only): deal each player a hand from the top of the deck, 9 cards with 3 players or 8 cards with 4 players. Undealt cards stay hidden and are not reshuffled.
2. Announce: everyone is told every player's face-up cards for this hand, every player's pudding count and score, and how many cards each hand holds. Each player is shown privately the cards in their own current hand.
3. Pick: all players at the same moment secretly choose one card from their own hand. If a hand holds one card, that card is taken automatically.
4. Reveal: all chosen cards are revealed at once and placed face up in front of their owners.
5. Record the chosen card:
   - Tempura adds 1 to your tempura count.
   - Sashimi adds 1 to your sashimi count.
   - Dumpling adds 1 to your dumpling count.
   - Maki adds its icons (1, 2 or 3) to your maki total.
   - Pudding adds 1 to your puddings, which are kept across all hands.
   - Wasabi adds 1 to your unused wasabi.
   - Nigiri is worth 1 (Egg), 2 (Salmon) or 3 (Squid). If you have at least 1 unused wasabi, the nigiri is placed on it: its value is tripled (3, 6 or 9) and your unused wasabi drops by 1. Add the nigiri's value to your nigiri points for this hand.
6. Pass: everyone passes their remaining hand to the player on their left.
7. Hand scoring (last pick of a hand only). Each player adds the following to their score:
   - Tempura: 5 points per complete pair, so floor(tempura/2) x 5.
   - Sashimi: 10 points per complete set of three, so floor(sashimi/3) x 10.
   - Dumplings: 0 for 0, 1 for 1, 3 for 2, 6 for 3, 10 for 4, and 15 for 5 or more.
   - Nigiri: all nigiri points for the hand. Unused wasabi scores 0.
   - Maki: among players with a maki total of at least 1, those with the highest total split 6 points equally, rounded down. If exactly one player has the highest total, the players with the second-highest total (at least 1) split 3 points equally, rounded down. If two or more players tie for highest, no second-place points are awarded.
   Then every hand-only count (tempura, sashimi, dumplings, maki, unused wasabi, nigiri points) resets to 0. Puddings stay.
8. Pudding scoring (last pick of the third hand only):
   - Players with the most puddings split +6 equally, rounded down.
   - Players with the fewest puddings split -6 equally, rounded toward zero (for example, two tied players get -3 each).
   - Players with 0 puddings count for the fewest.
   - If all players have the same number of puddings, nobody scores for pudding.
9. End check: after the last pick of the third hand, the game ends.

There is no talk phase.
variation.objective: After pudding scoring, the player with the highest score wins. If two or more players tie for the highest score, the one among them with the most puddings wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw among those players.
variation.expected_effect: Every turn is a choice that takes thought. Players weigh a card's value to their own sets against denying it to the left neighbour, who sees their hand next. They must remember which cards were in hands seen earlier to judge whether a missing tempura or third sashimi will come back around, and read neighbours' face-up cards to predict their picks. They must also balance the cross-hand pudding race against immediate points. Simple policies lose: grabbing the highest-value card leaves incomplete sets, chasing a single set is easily blocked, and ignoring pudding costs 6. Removing chopsticks and fixing 3-4 players makes the game buildable and slightly less luck-driven. Talk is left out: all picks are revealed anyway, and cheap claims about intentions would add words without a commitment worth testing.

balanced.evidence:
DECK CHECK: 14+14+14+6+12+8+10+5+5+10+6 = 104. Cards needed: 3 players x 9 x 3 hands = 81; 4 players x 8 x 3 hands = 96. Both fit in 104, so the deck never runs out.

PER-CARD VALUE TABLE (value if the set completes):
- Tempura: 2.5 per card, but 0 if it ends unpaired.
- Sashimi: 3.33 per card, but 0 unless it completes a triple.
- Dumpling: marginal value 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then 0 from the 6th; average 3 per card at 5.
- Nigiri: Egg 1, Salmon 2, Squid 3, or 3/6/9 on wasabi. Wasabi alone is worth 0; its value is the uplift it gives a later nigiri (+2 / +4 / +6).
- Maki: positional, 6 or 3 points split.
- Pudding: 0 now, a share of the +6/-6 swing at game end.

No option is strictly better whatever opponents do. Sashimi and tempura are worth 0 if opponents deny the set. Maki is worth 0 if outbid. The value of Squid depends on holding wasabi. The value of pudding depends on the others' counts.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule (highest score after pudding):
- 'Always first card in hand': the hand order is arbitrary, so this is effectively random drafting. It strands singleton tempura and partial sashimi. It averages roughly 15-25 points per hand, against 30-40 for a set-collecting drafter, and loses almost every game against sensible play.
- 'Always last card': same analysis.
- 'Always take pudding or maki when available': this wins the pudding +6 and some maki points, but forgoes sets worth about 10-20 points per hand. It loses to sensible play.
- 'Always the highest immediate face value' (Squid, then Salmon): nigiri alone yields about 6-12 points per hand. It loses to set collectors.
- None of these policies never loses. Against random players they sometimes win, but not almost always in a field of 3-4.

SEATS: picks are simultaneous and the passing direction is fixed and symmetric. Every seat receives from one neighbour and feeds the other, so there is no move-order edge. Information is symmetric (all tableaus public).

All players can realistically win. The labelled scoring numbers match the original Sushi Go.

playable.evidence:
RULES COVERAGE: every card has an explicit record rule.
- Wasabi: placement is automatic when unused wasabi is at least 1, which removes the original's choice ambiguity.
- Chopsticks: removed, which avoids a two-card pick.
- The last card is taken automatically.
- Maki: ties for first and second are defined, with rounding down (for example, 4-way tie for first gets 6/4 = 1 each, and no second place).
- Pudding: most and fewest are defined; ties are split with rounding toward zero; the all-equal case scores nothing. The '0 counts as fewest' clause is redundant but harmless.
- Hand-only counts reset after each hand; puddings persist.
- Winner: highest score, then most puddings, then a draw.

FINITENESS: 27 or 24 rounds, at most 40.

LIMITS:
- choice_steps_per_round: 1 simultaneous poll, at most 4.
- hidden_elements: 2 (deck and private hands), at most 3.
- random_draws_per_round: 1 (a single shuffle, then deals from the top), at most 1.
- attributes: 13 (score, puddings, tempura, sashimi, dumpling, maki, unused wasabi, nigiri points, hand, face-up cards and others), at most 20.

STEP ESTIMATE (fits 17 but is tight):
- deal 1, announce plus private view 1-2, pick 1, reveal 1, record 2 (sets/maki/pudding; nigiri+wasabi with if-ops), pass 1;
- hand scoring: tempura+sashimi 1, dumpling piecewise 1, nigiri 1, maki first 1, maki second 1, reset 1;
- pudding most 1, pudding fewest 1, end 1.
- Total is about 16-18. The engine's workarounds for maki ranking and the dumpling lookup are needed, and conditional `when`/`if` arithmetic supports them.

No board, clock, judge or trading is needed.

TALK: 3-4 players with conflicting interests, but a non-binding talk phase in a draft mostly adds words. Players can already infer each other's needs from public tableaus and passed hands, so they are not reduced to guessing. Omitting talk is a sensible choice.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT THERE IS TO INFER: with 3 players a 9-card hand returns to you after 3 picks. You see the hand's contents again and can deduce what each neighbour took, since all chosen cards are revealed. From that you can track:
- which sets each opponent is building (two sashimi means they want the third);
- maki standings;
- pudding race standings.

WAYS TO ACT ON IT:
- Hate-drafting: deny the completing sashimi or tempura.
- Timing: take wasabi early only if Squid or Salmon is likely to come round.
- Abandoning lost races: stop chasing maki or pudding when hopeless.
- Planning: across 3 hands for pudding.

CHANCE: from the initial deal, roughly 25-35% of the outcome variance between equal-skill players; a strong hand can be partly countered by neighbours.

ALL PLAY WELL: when all play the intended strategy, the winner is decided by marginal drafting and denial choices across 24-27 picks, not by the deal alone.

SKILLED VS UNSKILLED: a skilled drafter reliably outscores an unskilled one by about 15-30 points per game. Reasoning is clearly favoured.
